items.stem:
Read the following memoir extract by a writer remembering her first day in a new country.

I was nine when we arrived in Oslo in January. I had never seen snow, and I had never been so cold that my teeth hurt.
My mother bought me a red coat from a charity shop. It was two sizes too big. 'You will grow into it,' she said, and she was right, though not in the way she meant.
That coat went everywhere with me – to my first Norwegian lesson, to my first sleepover, to the school where nobody could say my name.
I still have it. It fits now. So does the city.

Identify one detail that reflects the context of the extract and explain its significance.
items.answer: The writer was a nine-year-old migrant arriving in Norway in winter; the cold, the new language and the name nobody could pronounce show the challenges of migration.
items.markingKey: The writer was a nine-year-old migrant arriving in Norway in winter; the cold, the new language and the name nobody could pronounce show the challenges of migration. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a contemporary novel about a refugee student in Berlin.

On the first day, the teacher wrote my name on the board wrong. Nobody corrected her, so I didn't either.
Now, six months later, everyone calls me Sami instead of Samir, and I answer to it like a dog answers to a whistle.
In history we studied walls – the Berlin Wall, how it divided families. Lena put up her hand and said, "At least that's all in the past."
I thought of my uncle, still on the other side of a border, still waiting. I didn't put up my hand.

Explain how the historical or social context of this extract shapes its meaning.
items.answer: Contemporary context: Germany received many refugees in the 2010s; the setting in Berlin, a city once divided by a wall, makes the theme of borders especially resonant.
items.markingKey: Contemporary context: Germany received many refugees in the 2010s; the setting in Berlin, a city once divided by a wall, makes the theme of borders especially resonant. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

Answer the following question in a well-organised response of about 250 words: How does the writer present Samir's experience of belonging and not belonging?

The repeated silences frame the extract, showing that he belongs on the surface but keeps his real self hidden.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel set in Alabama in 1955.

The bus was crowded and hot. Ruth sat in the middle section with her mother, behind the painted line, where coloured passengers were allowed to sit if no white passenger needed the seat.
At the third stop a man got on. There was nowhere for him to sit.
The driver looked in the mirror. "Y'all better make it light on yourselves," he said.
Ruth felt her mother's hand tighten on hers. Three people stood up. Her mother did not.
Ruth had never heard silence so loud.

Explain what the character's actions and words reveal about them.
items.answer: Ruth's mother is quietly courageous: she stays seated despite the threat. Ruth is a child observer who senses danger through her mother's tightening hand and the "loud" silence.
items.markingKey: Ruth's mother is quietly courageous: she stays seated despite the threat. Ruth is a child observer who senses danger through her mother's tightening hand and the "loud" silence. items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel set in Alabama in 1955.

The bus was crowded and hot. Ruth sat in the middle section with her mother, behind the painted line, where coloured passengers were allowed to sit if no white passenger needed the seat.
At the third stop a man got on. There was nowhere for him to sit.
The driver looked in the mirror. "Y'all better make it light on yourselves," he said.
Ruth felt her mother's hand tighten on hers. Three people stood up. Her mother did not.
Ruth had never heard silence so loud.

What message or theme does the writer explore here? Support your answer with evidence.
items.answer: Theme: injustice and quiet resistance. How it is developed: Seen through Ruth, the injustice is shown rather than explained: the "painted line" symbolises segregation, and the driver's casual threat reveals how prejudice was normalised. Ruth senses danger physically ("her mother's hand tighten"), and the contrast "Three people stood up. Her mother did not." isolates the act of resistance. The oxymoron "silence so loud" captures the tension a child feels but cannot fully name; the historical context of Montgomery in 1955 makes the mother's courage resonate with real resistance.
items.markingKey: Theme: injustice and quiet resistance. How it is developed: Seen through Ruth, the injustice is shown rather than explained: the "painted line" symbolises segregation, and the driver's casual threat reveals how prejudice was normalised. Ruth senses danger physically ("her mother's hand tighten"), and the contrast "Three people stood up. Her mother did not." isolates the act of resistance. The oxymoron "silence so loud" captures the tension a child feels but cannot fully name; the historical context of Montgomery in 1955 makes the mother's courage resonate with real resistance. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel about starting a new school.

Mei stood at the classroom door clutching a timetable she had folded so many times it was soft as cloth.
Twenty-eight faces turned. Someone laughed – not at her, probably, but her cheeks burned anyway.
"There's a seat here," said a girl with silver braces and paint on her fingers. She shoved a pile of comics aside. "I'm Zara. Do you like drawing? Please say yes. Nobody here likes drawing."
Mei, who had filled three sketchbooks on the plane from Shanghai, almost smiled.
"Yes," she said. It was the first word she had spoken all day.

How does the writer present Mei's feelings on her first day at a new school?
Write a PEEL paragraph that answers the question, with at least one embedded quotation.
items.answer: Point: Mei is presented as anxious and isolated. Evidence: the timetable folded until "soft as cloth" and her "cheeks burned anyway". Explanation: the simile reveals repeated nervous handling and the physical blush shows embarrassment even when she is not sure she is being mocked ("probably"). The short sentence "Twenty-eight faces turned" emphasises sudden attention. Zara's chatter about drawing creates hope, and the final line reveals that "Yes" is her first word all day, a turning point towards belonging.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Point: Mei is presented as anxious and isolated. Evidence: the timetable folded until "soft as cloth" and her "cheeks burned anyway". Explanation: the simile reveals repeated nervous handling and the physical blush shows embarrassment even when she is not sure she is being mocked ("probably"). The short sentence "Twenty-eight faces turned" emphasises sudden attention. Zara's chatter about drawing creates hope, and the final line reveals that "Yes" is her first word all day, a turning point towards belonging. items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel set in Soweto, South Africa, in 1976.

The new rule came on a Monday: half our subjects would now be taught in Afrikaans. Mathematics. Geography. A language most of our teachers barely spoke.
Thabo tore the notice from the classroom door. "They want to teach us in the language of the people who made the pass laws," he said.
I said nothing. I was fourteen and I wanted to pass my exams.
By June I was marching beside him, holding a cardboard sign: WE ARE NOT AFRAID. My hands were shaking so much the letters blurred.

What message or theme does the writer explore here? Support your answer with evidence.
items.answer: Theme: education, language and resistance. How it is developed: At first the narrator is passive ("I said nothing") and focused on exams, contrasting with Thabo's defiance. The time jump "By June" shows rapid change, and the image of marching with the sign "WE ARE NOT AFRAID" while his hands shake uses irony to show courage alongside fear. The 1976 Soweto context gives the personal change historical weight.
items.markingKey: Theme: education, language and resistance. How it is developed: At first the narrator is passive ("I said nothing") and focused on exams, contrasting with Thabo's defiance. The time jump "By June" shows rapid change, and the image of marching with the sign "WE ARE NOT AFRAID" while his hands shake uses irony to show courage alongside fear. The 1976 Soweto context gives the personal change historical weight. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

At the third stop a man got on. There was nowhere for him to sit.
The driver looked in the mirror. "Y'all better make it light on yourselves," he said.
Ruth felt her mother's hand tighten on hers. Three people stood up. Her mother did not.
Ruth had never heard silence so loud.

Essay question: How does the writer use a child's perspective to present injustice in this extract? Write the introduction (with a thesis) and your first body paragraph.
items.answer: Seen through Ruth, the injustice is shown rather than explained: the "painted line" symbolises segregation, and the driver's casual threat reveals how prejudice was normalised. Ruth senses danger physically ("her mother's hand tighten"), and the contrast "Three people stood up. Her mother did not." isolates the act of resistance. The oxymoron "silence so loud" captures the tension a child feels but cannot fully name; the historical context of Montgomery in 1955 makes the mother's courage resonate with real resistance.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Seen through Ruth, the injustice is shown rather than explained: the "painted line" symbolises segregation, and the driver's casual threat reveals how prejudice was normalised. Ruth senses danger physically ("her mother's hand tighten"), and the contrast "Three people stood up. Her mother did not." isolates the act of resistance. The oxymoron "silence so loud" captures the tension a child feels but cannot fully name; the historical context of Montgomery in 1955 makes the mother's courage resonate with real resistance. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel set in Soweto, South Africa, in 1976.

The new rule came on a Monday: half our subjects would now be taught in Afrikaans. Mathematics. Geography. A language most of our teachers barely spoke.
Thabo tore the notice from the classroom door. "They want to teach us in the language of the people who made the pass laws," he said.
I said nothing. I was fourteen and I wanted to pass my exams.
By June I was marching beside him, holding a cardboard sign: WE ARE NOT AFRAID. My hands were shaking so much the letters blurred.

Identify one detail that reflects the context of the extract and explain its significance.
items.answer: Historical context: in 1976 the apartheid government ordered that Afrikaans be used to teach some subjects in Black schools; on 16 June 1976 thousands of Soweto students protested, and police opened fire. The extract shows how education became a site of resistance.
items.markingKey: Historical context: in 1976 the apartheid government ordered that Afrikaans be used to teach some subjects in Black schools; on 16 June 1976 thousands of Soweto students protested, and police opened fire. The extract shows how education became a site of resistance. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Suggest a symbol a writer could use in a novel about a family divided by a border, and explain its meaning.
items.answer: E.g. a broken phone line or an empty chair at the table, representing the absent relative and the family's incompleteness.

items.stem: Ingrid writes: "An analytical essay should retell the plot so the examiner knows what happens." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The examiner knows the plot; analysis explains how and why the writer creates meaning, using brief references.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "A novel about prejudice cannot be understood without knowing its historical context."
items.answer: Context greatly deepens understanding, but powerful novels also communicate universal experiences that readers can grasp before researching the history.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: context explains laws and dangers; readers may misread characters' choices. Arguments against: universal emotions of fear and courage are understandable anyway; good novels provide context within the story. Supported judgement: Context greatly deepens understanding, but powerful novels also communicate universal experiences that readers can grasp before researching the history.

items.stem: "Readers learn most about injustice from characters who change." Discuss.
items.answer: Changing characters model growth, but static characters can reveal the stubbornness of prejudice; both teach readers.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: change shows how understanding develops; readers identify with growth. Arguments against: static characters can show how deeply prejudice is rooted; victims' unchanging resilience can be powerful. Supported judgement: Changing characters model growth, but static characters can reveal the stubbornness of prejudice; both teach readers. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Symbols are more powerful than direct statements in novels about injustice."
items.answer: Symbols often create deeper, lasting impact, but direct moments of testimony are also powerful; the best novels combine both.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they engage readers to interpret; they are memorable and layered. Arguments against: direct statements can be clear and urgent; some readers may miss symbols.
